name: Oxandrolone
lead: Oxandrolone, widely known by the brand name Anavar, is an oral synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) derived from dihydrotestosterone. A 17-alpha-methyl group allows it to be taken by mouth, and an oxygen atom replaces a carbon in its A ring, a structural feature that makes it unusual among steroids.[1][20] It is reported to have several times the anabolic potency of testosterone with only a small fraction of its androgenic potency, which is why it became the AAS most often given to children, women and older patients.[20]

For appearance, people use it to build or hold lean muscle and to look dry and defined during a cut, with comparatively little water retention and no conversion to oestrogen.[2][5][20] In looksmaxxing forums it is also discussed by teenagers who hope to extend growth while their growth plates are open, a use that the paediatric literature describes in more nuanced terms.[3][6][1]

Unlike most compounds in its class, oxandrolone has substantial randomised trial data, mainly in burns, trauma, HIV wasting, alcoholic hepatitis and growth disorders, reporting effects on weight, lean mass and wound healing in patients.[7][8][9][11][20] Controlled trials in healthy people aimed at appearance have not been published. The US Food and Drug Administration withdrew approval of the drug for all indications in 2023, citing safety and effectiveness concerns, after its brand had already left the market.[20]
infobox: 1962 (Raphael Pappo and Christopher Jung, Searle Laboratories)[20]
US approval withdrawn 2023; controlled substance in many countries; prohibited in sport[20]

paras: Oxandrolone was labelled to promote weight gain after extensive surgery, chronic infection or severe trauma, to counter catabolism from long-term corticosteroids, and to relieve bone pain from osteoporosis.[1][20] It was also used in HIV wasting, in alcoholic hepatitis with malnutrition, and in growth disorders including constitutional delay of growth and puberty and Turner syndrome.[1][4][20]

Burn care became its best-known clinical setting. Meta-analyses summarised in encyclopedic sources report less catabolic weight loss, more lean body mass, faster donor-site healing and shorter intensive-care and hospital stays in severely burned patients, and reviews of burn nutrition discuss it as a metabolic adjunct.[10][20][22][23] In Turner syndrome, a 2019 Cochrane review is described as finding moderate-quality evidence that adding it to growth hormone increased adult height, though growth hormone alone largely replaced it by the mid-2010s.[20]

Non-medical users take it, often with testosterone, for lean mass gain and fat loss without much water retention; looksmax.org users describe it as good for cutting and as a milder add-on to a first cycle.[2][5] Wikipedia notes that because it is more anabolic than androgenic it has been favoured by women and by people seeking milder steroid regimens, and that its reputation for low liver toxicity once added to its appeal.[20] T Nation posters have described it as one of the most potently anabolic steroids milligram for milligram and discuss it in both male and female contexts.[19]

Some young posters ask whether it can extend growth while growth plates are open, sometimes citing small paediatric trials from the 1980s and 1990s that measured growth velocity in boys with delayed growth.[3][6] These threads also attract replies warning about hormonal suppression and urging a testosterone base, illustrating that the forum community itself is divided on the idea.[3]

Oxandrolone is an agonist of the androgen receptor, the target of testosterone and dihydrotestosterone. Activating the receptor increases protein synthesis, lean mass and bone mineral density, and its binding to the receptor is relatively weak compared with some synthetic steroids.[20] It cannot be converted into oestrogen by aromatase, which is why gynaecomastia is not generally associated with it.[20]

Oral bioavailability is about 97 percent and plasma protein binding about 94 to 97 percent.[20] Unusually for a 17-alpha-alkylated steroid it is described as metabolised largely by the kidneys rather than the liver, and about 28 percent of a dose appears unchanged in urine.[20] The elimination half-life is about 9 to 10 hours in adults and longer in the elderly.[20]

Oxandrolone is 2-oxa-17-alpha-methyl-dihydrotestosterone. Related steroids include mestanolone, oxymetholone and stanozolol.[20] The 17-alpha-methyl group allows oral use but is associated with liver strain across the class.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial gave oxandrolone to 62 multiple-trauma patients on enteral nutrition for up to 28 days.[7] A multicentre randomised trial studied it in AIDS-wasting myopathy,[8] and a study of anabolic effects after severe burn was published in the Annals of Surgery in 2001.[9] A 2004 Lancet review of the metabolic response to burn injury discusses anabolic strategies for severe burns, and a 2005 review covers post-burn muscle wasting and its treatments.[22][23] Reviews of burn nutrition and metabolic support discuss oxandrolone as an adjunct.[10] An encyclopedic overview cites meta-analyses in severe burns reporting reduced weight loss and faster donor-site healing, and a trial in older men reporting lean mass gain over 12 weeks.[1][20]

Older studies examined alcoholic hepatitis. A Veterans Affairs cooperative study of 273 men combined oxandrolone with an enteral food supplement; on an intention-to-treat basis mortality changed only minimally, though differences were reported in a subgroup with moderate malnutrition.[11] A 1984 study examined survival with oxandrolone and prednisolone, and a later re-examination of two Veterans Administration studies related protein-calorie malnutrition to outcomes.[12][24] A plastic-surgery review summarises the drug's use in reconstructive and burn settings.[21]

Growth studies include randomised trials in boys with Klinefelter syndrome, one reporting an increased risk of early gonadarche[13] and another examining effects on hippocampus structure,[25] plus trials in Turner syndrome including androgen-responsive aspects of cognition.[4][26] An early preliminary analysis examined oxandrolone in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.[27] An encyclopedic source states that low-dose treatment raised height velocity in boys with constitutional delay but accelerated bone maturation, with adult height not differing from controls in long-term follow-up.[1]

No trial of oxandrolone for cosmetic muscle gain or appearance in healthy people was found. Registered studies include injury rehabilitation (ACL reconstruction, multiligament knee and rotator cuff repair),[14][15][28] spinal cord injury,[29] infant growth and malnutrition,[30][31] and a phase 1 bioavailability study in healthy adults.[16]

Reported risks of the AAS class include liver toxicity, cardiovascular effects and hormonal disruption, and oxandrolone is stated to carry them despite its mild androgenic profile.[1] Its label and encyclopedic summaries describe peliosis hepatis (sometimes with liver failure or intra-abdominal bleeding), liver tumours, cholestatic hepatitis, adverse blood lipid changes linked to atherosclerosis risk, and prostate effects in older men.[20] Elevated liver enzymes have been observed with high doses or prolonged treatment, sometimes normalising after stopping.[20]

Women may experience virilisation, which can be irreversible, so doses in women and children are kept low and monitored; like other androgens it can worsen acne and lower male fertility by suppressing the body's own testosterone production.[20] Oxandrolone strongly increases the effect of the anticoagulant warfarin, prompting a 2004 safety alert from its then manufacturer, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy because of possible fetal masculinisation.[20] A 1991 report described adolescent boys with gynaecomastia, many of whom needed surgery.[20] A case report described delayed rhabdomyolysis in a person using AAS.[17] Nutritional supplement analyses have found products cross-contaminated with or faked to contain doping substances, which affects people buying unregulated products.[18]

Oxandrolone was a US Schedule III controlled substance, was scheduled in Canada (2017) and the UK, and is prohibited in sport.[1][20] T Nation posters note that prescriptions for high doses of oxandrolone, testosterone and similar drugs sit in a legal grey area.[19]

After Searle discontinued Anavar in 1989, partly due to bad publicity from bodybuilding use, the rights passed to Bio-Technology General (later Savient), which relaunched it as Oxandrin in 1995.[20] A manufacturer asked the FDA to withdraw approval in March 2019, the agency notified licence holders in December 2022 that it should be removed, and approval for all indications was withdrawn in 2023.[20]

Oxandrolone threads on looksmax.org range from cutting and first-cycle questions to heightmaxxing, with titles such as 'anavar is a wonder steroid' and comparisons to other steroids.[2][3][5][32][33] T Nation members discuss it in training logs and cycle-planning threads.[34] The gray-market and counterfeit-product concerns in the wider supplement literature are relevant to these communities.[18]

Current registered work centres on injury recovery, including a phase 2 study of an implanted pellet after ACL reconstruction and a suspended phase 4 multiligament knee study, and on paediatric growth and nutrition in congenital heart disease and infant malnutrition.[14][28][30][31] Reviews of persistent inflammation, immunosuppression and catabolism syndrome and of ICU nutrition discuss anabolic agents as a research question in critical illness.[35][36]

timeline.event: First synthesised by Pappo and Jung at Searle Laboratories.[1][20]
Introduced for medical use as Anavar in the United States.[1][20]
An FDA advisory committee review questioned the osteoporosis indication; a New England Journal of Medicine study of oxandrolone in alcoholic hepatitis appeared the same year.[1][12][20]
Searle discontinued Anavar, partly because of publicity about illicit bodybuilding use.[20]
Veterans Affairs cooperative study of oxandrolone in malnourished alcoholic hepatitis patients published.[11]
Savient (then Bio-Technology General) released it as Oxandrin.[20]
Annals of Surgery trial reported anabolic effects after severe burn.[9]
Manufacturer issued a safety alert on the warfarin interaction.[20]
Marketing holder asked the FDA to withdraw approval; a Cochrane review on Turner syndrome appeared.[20]
FDA withdrew approval for all indications.[20]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org oxandrolone is regarded as a mild, 'wonder' steroid and is repeatedly discussed in height-focused threads by teenagers; T Nation members discuss it in training logs and for women.[3][5][6][19][32]

claims.claim: Anavar can add height or complement growth hormone in teens.
claims.believers: A 16-year-old with delayed bone age cites paediatric trials in which oxandrolone raised growth velocity and plans to use it; a 14-year-old asks about adding it to growth hormone.[3][6]
claims.experts: An encyclopedic overview says low-dose treatment raised height velocity in boys with constitutional delay but accelerated bone maturation, with adult height not differing from controls in long-term follow-up; higher doses are said to risk early growth plate closure.[1]

claims.believers: A poster says it lets users reach very low body fat, comparing it favourably to cardarine as 'more tested and safer'.[5]
claims.experts: Trials show reduced weight loss and lean mass preservation in burns and wasting.[1][7] No trials in healthy people cutting for appearance were found.

claims.claim: Anavar is a mild addition to a first test cycle.
claims.believers: Threads ask if there is any reason not to add it to a first testosterone cycle, treating it as low-risk.[2]
claims.experts: Reviews list liver and cardiovascular risks for AAS generally, and the oxandrolone overview says it carries the class's risks.[1]

claims.claim: Anavar is easy on the liver compared with other orals.
claims.believers: Posters and the older bodybuilding reputation describe it as the milder oral, and threads treat it as a low-risk add-on.[2][20]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says that for years oxandrolone was thought uniquely free of liver toxicity, but documented peliosis hepatis and liver tumours contributed to the FDA's 2023 withdrawal.[20]

claims.claim: Women can use it with little virilisation.
claims.believers: T Nation posters describe low-dose oxandrolone as the usual first steroid for women.[19]
claims.experts: Clinical sources state virilisation can occur and may be irreversible, and doses in women are minimised and monitored.[20]

claims.claim: A doctor can legally prescribe high doses.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says supra-physiological prescriptions of oxandrolone and testosterone are possible as a 'legal loophole'.[19]
claims.experts: The FDA withdrew approval of oxandrolone for all indications in 2023, so it is no longer an approved US product.[20]

card.summary: An oral steroid with real clinical trial data in burns and wasting, popular as a mild cutting drug; its height claims conflict with growth studies.
card.note: Trial benefits are in patients; teen height use contradicts the growth literature; liver and cardiac risks apply.

quick.overview:
Oxandrolone (Anavar) is an oral anabolic steroid made in the 1960s. It has been prescribed to restore weight after burns, trauma and surgery, and some people use it for a lean, dry physique.

Unusually for the category, it has randomised trials in patients showing weight and lean mass benefits. There are no controlled trials in healthy people for appearance. Teen forum posts discuss it for height, but growth studies show faster bone maturation without taller adult height, per an encyclopedic source.
quick.mechanism: It activates the androgen receptor, with relatively mild androgenic effect. The 17-alpha-methyl group allows oral use but is tied to liver strain.
quick.risks: Class risks include liver toxicity, cardiovascular effects and hormonal suppression. It is US Schedule III and banned in sport, and unregulated products can be contaminated or fake.

angle.text: Users take oxandrolone to add or preserve muscle and to look drier and more defined while dieting, often alongside testosterone. Patient trials show gains in lean mass and weight, and its low oestrogenic activity is the reason users cite for a 'dry' look.
